newsitem.title: PERU: Peru looks abroad for ways to revive hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru looks abroad for ways to revive hostage talks.

text.p: With talks to end Peru's 106-day hostage crisis stalled, President Alberto Fujimori has decided to look abroad for ideas on how to free the 72 captives.

Fujimori will visit Bolivia, whose ambassador is one of the hostages inside the Japanese diplomatic residence, while Congress President Victor Joy Way will go to Tokyo early next week for talks with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Talks will focus on the government's negotiation strategy, about which "there is full agreement not only at a national but at an international level," Joy Way told reporters.

Japan's ambassador Morihisa Aoki was hosting a reception when Marxist guerrillas stormed the house on Dec. 17, taking 500 VIPs captive. Most were soon freed. The remaining hostages include Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Peruvian cabinet ministers and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
Fujimori will fly on Saturday to La Paz for talks with Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada.

On Monday, after a telephone chat with Fujimori, Sanchez de Lozada said the Peruvian leader did not believe there would be a rapid solution to the standoff due to "new disagreements" with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
The MRTA has renewed demands for the release of 450 jailed members before it frees any hostages. Fujimori has rejected this demand and insisted he will not cave in to pressure.
Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina, whose country has offered asylum to the 20-odd hostage-takers to help end the standoff, is also expected to visit Japan in the coming days.

Japan's news agency Jiji Press quoted a government source in Tokyo as saying Robaina is expected to exchange views on the hostage crisis with his counterpart Yukihiko Ikeda and other Japanese government officials on April 17.
The agency said Tokyo was studying economic cooperation and aid for Cuba after the solution of the crisis.

Speculation in Lima that the MRTA was prepared to accept Cuba's asylum offer, a ransom payment and the release of only some low-ranking MRTA prisoners raised hopes last week that the crisis would be solved quickly and peacefully.

But tough statements over the Easter holiday by Fujimori and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa -- who insisted on the release of the prisoners and denied he and his rebels were ready to leave the country -- shattered that optimism.

In the latest exchange, the MRTA said in a statement issued on Wednesday that a reported riot at a maximum security jail last week was a government fabrication aimed at paving the way for the killing of political inmates.
"We denounce this act as a preparation maneuver to justify the murder of political prisoners," said an MRTA statment posted on the Internet by its international arm in Germany.
On Thursday, police said they quelled a riot at the Castro Castro prison but called it a minor incident that had erupted when relatives were denied special visiting hours for Easter.
Despite the low point in talks, Tuesday saw unusually intense activity, including a seven-hour meeting between Cipriani and government negotiator Domingo Palermo.
The two other guarantors, Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, spent several hours inside the besieged residence with the MRTA.
While the mediators have been busy, the government and the MRTA have not met face-to-face since March 12 and no new talks are on the agenda.
The slow pace has added to concern about the hostages' physical and mental health, and about their relations with their captors.

"The terrorists themselves are deteriorating emotionally, and that could lead to a violent outcome," Congresswoman Marta Chavez told Reuters. Fujimori has warned that he may use force if the MRTA harms the hostages in any way.
